blurb.heading: Sixty-two years under. Seven days above.
paragraphs: In 1963 the village of Undercleeve was emptied, blessed, and drowned beneath a new reservoir, and Iris Aldous — its last postmistress — dropped her door key into the rising water rather than hand it over. For sixty-one years she lived above the dam, watching the lake the way other people watch a locked room.

Now Iris is gone, a record drought has pulled the water back, and for one week the county is opening the shore to the families. Her granddaughter Nell, a paper conservator who spends her days rescuing other people’s histories from water damage, drives west with a sealed box she was never told the meaning of — and finds, on the drying bed of the lake, a door standing open that should have fallen sixty years ago, and one line of footprints going in.

What the River Keeps is a novel about the weight of inherited silence: about the things institutions take, the things families refuse to surrender, and what rises when the water finally gives its hostages back.

quotes.quote: A debut with the patience of deep water. Halloran writes loss the way engineers build dams — quietly, and to hold.
quotes.source: Jude Merrow, author of The Salt Meadow

quotes.quote: The best kind of ghost story: one where the ghost is a village, and the haunting is done by paperwork, kindness, and a bent weathervane.
I finished the first chapter standing up in my kitchen and did not notice. Buy it for the atmosphere; keep it for Iris.

author.heading: Nora Halloran
bio: Nora Halloran grew up in a market town at the mouth of a flooded valley, where her grandmother kept a framed photograph of a high street nobody could visit. She trained as an archivist and spent a decade cataloguing parish records, compensation ledgers, and other paperwork of quiet catastrophes — the raw material that eventually became this book.
What the River Keeps is her first novel. She lives within walking distance of a reservoir and checks the waterline more often than the forecast.

items.question: Is this the whole book?
items.answer: No — this site carries chapter one in full, exactly as it appears in the finished novel, and nothing past it. If you reach the last line and want chapter two, that is what the buy button is for.

items.question: Where can I buy the full novel?
items.answer: Through the buy button on this page, which goes straight to the bookshop that stocks it. Your local bookshop can also order it by title and author. This site itself sells nothing and never asks for payment details.

items.question: What formats does the book come in?
items.answer: Paperback and ebook, with both editions listed on the same shop page. The chapter you read here is set from the same text as the print edition.

items.question: Can I share this chapter with someone?
items.answer: Please do — send them the link to this page. The chapter is free to read in the browser for anyone, and your reading position is saved only on your own device.
